title: Heat Transfer Methods
lead: Heat passes quickly through a cooking pan and slowly through the walls of a picnic ice chest, and we slow or speed it by the materials we choose, the air we let move and the color we paint a roof. Every such transfer takes place by one of only three methods. This section defines them: conduction, through matter that stays in place; convection, by the movement of a fluid; and radiation, by electromagnetic waves that need no matter at all. A fireplace shows all three at once, and a thermos bottle is built to slow every one of them.
objectives: Discuss the different methods of heat transfer.
summary_html: • Heat is transferred by three different methods: conduction, convection, and radiation.

figures.original_caption: In a fireplace, heat transfer occurs by all three methods: conduction, convection, and radiation. Radiation is responsible for most of the heat transferred into the room. Heat transfer also occurs through conduction into the room, but at a much slower rate. Heat transfer by convection also occurs through cold air entering the room around windows and hot air leaving the room by rising up the chimney.
The construction of a thermos bottle is designed to inhibit all methods of heat transfer.

exercises.prompt: Name an example from daily life (different from the text) for each mechanism of heat transfer.

answer.solution:
Conduction: Heat transfers into your hands as you hold a hot cup of coffee.
Convection: Heat transfers as the barista “steams” cold milk to make hot cocoa.
Radiation: Reheating a cold cup of coffee in a microwave oven.

exercises.prompt: What are the main methods of heat transfer from the hot core of Earth to its surface? From Earth’s surface to outer space?

answer.solution: Ask, for each stage, what lies between the hot body and the cold one. Between the core and the surface there is rock, some of it solid and some of it able to flow slowly over long times. Through the solid rock heat moves by conduction, since the matter stays in place and the heat passes through it by contact; where the rock of the mantle flows, and where molten rock rises toward the surface in volcanic regions, the moving material carries its heat with it, which is convection. Between the surface and outer space there is, beyond the atmosphere, nothing at all. Conduction and convection both need matter, so neither can carry heat across empty space, and the only method left is radiation: the Earth’s surface and atmosphere emit infrared radiation, which travels outward with nothing to carry it, exactly as the Sun’s light reaches the Earth.

exercises.prompt: When our bodies get too warm, they respond by sweating and increasing blood circulation to the surface to transfer thermal energy away from the core. What effect will this have on a person in a $40.0^\circ\text{C}$ hot tub?

answer.solution: Begin with the rule that governs every method: heat is transferred only because of a temperature difference, and it goes from the hotter body to the colder one. The body’s core is near $37^\circ\text{C}$, and the water is at $40.0^\circ\text{C}$, so the water is the hotter body. Bringing more blood to the skin is convection within the body; it moves the blood, and the heat it carries, between the core and the surface. In cool air the skin is colder than the core and this carries heat outward, but in the hot tub the skin is in contact with water warmer than the core, so the circulating blood picks up heat at the skin and carries it inward instead. The response works against the person. Sweating cannot help either, because sweat cools the skin only by evaporating, and skin under water cannot dry. The person keeps warming up, which is why time in a hot tub has to be limited.

exercises.prompt: Figure 14.14 shows a cut-away drawing of a thermos bottle (also known as a Dewar flask), which is a device designed specifically to slow down all forms of heat transfer. Explain the functions of the various parts, such as the vacuum, the silvering of the walls, the thin-walled long glass neck, the rubber support, the air layer, and the stopper.

answer.solution: Take each part and ask which of the three methods it stands in the way of. The vacuum between the two glass walls contains almost no matter, and conduction and convection both need matter, so neither can carry heat across it; that leaves only radiation to cross the gap. The silvering of the walls answers radiation: a shiny surface emits little radiation and reflects most of what falls on it, so the radiation that leaves the inner wall is small and is largely turned back. The liquid is connected to the outside only through the glass of the neck, and the neck is long and thin-walled so that the path for conduction through the glass is as long and as narrow as can be, which keeps that conduction slow. The rubber support and the spring centering device touch the vessel only at small points, and rubber is a poor conductor, so very little heat is conducted through the mountings. The layer of air between the vessel and the outer container is a poor conductor too, and being enclosed it cannot circulate much, so conduction and convection through it are both small. The stopper closes the mouth so that the warm air above the liquid cannot rise out and be replaced by cold air, which would be convection, and it is made of a poor conductor so that little heat passes through it by conduction.
